candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — piperacillin-tazobactam mechanism and antimicrobial stewardship
candidate.educational_objective: Describe piperacillin-tazobactam as a penicillin-class antibacterial plus beta-lactamase inhibitor: piperacillin inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, while tazobactam inhibits certain beta-lactamases and does not eliminate the need to use susceptibility information when available.

options.A: Piperacillin inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, while tazobactam inhibits certain beta-lactamases that can inactivate beta-lactam antibiotics.
options.B: Tazobactam is the primary bactericidal component, while piperacillin mainly prevents renal elimination of tazobactam.
options.C: The combination is an antiviral regimen whose activity depends on blocking viral nucleic-acid replication.
options.D: Tazobactam eliminates all clinically important beta-lactamase-mediated resistance, so culture and susceptibility data do not affect therapy.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. The current DailyMed prescribing information states that piperacillin exerts bactericidal activity by inhibiting bacterial septum formation and cell-wall synthesis, while tazobactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor with little clinically relevant antibacterial activity by itself. B reverses the roles of the two components. C is incorrect because piperacillin-tazobactam is an antibacterial combination, not an antiviral drug. D is incorrect because tazobactam inhibits specified classes of beta-lactamases rather than every resistance mechanism, and the label directs clinicians to consider culture and susceptibility information when available when selecting or modifying therapy.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Piperacillin provides bactericidal cell-wall synthesis inhibition, while tazobactam inhibits certain beta-lactamases; the combination remains subject to organism susceptibility and culture-guided modification when data are available.
